lead: Most columns carry a moment as well as an axial load: from beams on one side only, from wind, or simply from the minimum eccentricity. Load and moment cannot be checked separately, because a little axial compression actually helps a section resist bending while a lot of it hurts. The interaction diagram draws this as one curve of P<sub>u</sub> against M<sub>u</sub> for a given section and steel; a load case is safe if its point lies inside. SP 16 prints these curves in non-dimensional form, and for moments about both axes IS 456 adds a simple load-contour check.
prereq: You need the axial formula and bar rules from Axially loaded short columns, and strain compatibility with the stress block 0.36fckb xu acting at 0.42xu (see Stress block parameters for limit state of collapse).

sections.h3: How the interaction diagram is built

blocks.text: Pick a depth x<sub>u</sub> of the neutral axis. Strain is 0.0035 at the compressed face and varies linearly (when x<sub>u</sub> is larger than D, the code instead fixes 0.002 at 3D/7 from the compressed face). Each bar gets its strain, then its stress from the design stress–strain curve of the steel. Adding the concrete force and the bar forces gives P<sub>u</sub>; taking their moments about the centroid gives M<sub>u</sub>. Repeating for many x<sub>u</sub> traces the curve.

items: Pure axial load (xu → ∞): Puz = 0.45fckAc + 0.75fyAsc. The design cap for any column is the axial formula 0.4fckAc + 0.67fyAsc, which already allows for emin.
Balanced point: the tension steel reaches 0.87fy/Es + 0.002 (0.0038 for Fe415) as the concrete reaches 0.0035. The moment capacity is near its largest here.
Compression failure above the balanced load: more Pu means less Mu. Tension failure below it: more Pu means more Mu, because compression delays yielding of the tension steel.
Pure bending (Pu = 0): the section behaves as a doubly reinforced beam.

blocks.text: SP 16 plots P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD) against M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD²) with one curve per value of p/f<sub>ck</sub> (p is the steel percentage), for Fe250, Fe415 and Fe500, for d′/D = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15 and 0.20, and for bars on two faces or spread round four faces. Circular columns have their own charts. The design procedure is: compute the two non-dimensional numbers, read p/f<sub>ck</sub>, and find A<sub>sc</sub> = p b D/100.
A corner column bends about both axes. IS 456 clause 39.6 uses the load-contour method (often called Bresler's method):

blocks.where: Mux, Muy are the factored moments about x and y (each at least Puemin); Mux1, Muy1 are the uniaxial moment capacities about x and y at the same Pu; αn = 1.0 when Pu/Puz ≤ 0.2, 2.0 when Pu/Puz ≥ 0.8, and linear in between: αn = 1 + (Pu/Puz − 0.2)/0.6.

items: Find P<sub>u</sub>, M<sub>ux</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub>; raise each moment to at least P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub>.
Assume bars spread round four faces; take a trial p (often 1.5 to 2.5 %).
Read or compute M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> at P<sub>u</sub>.
Check the load contour; if the sum exceeds 1, increase p and repeat.

blocks.text: A circular section with equally spaced bars is symmetric about every diameter, so moments about two axes combine into one: M<sub>u</sub> = √(M<sub>ux</sub>² + M<sub>uy</sub>²), checked as uniaxial bending. Use at least 6 bars. The capacity changes slightly with how the bars sit relative to the bending axis; design charts use the weaker orientation.

examples.question: A braced short column 300 mm × 500 mm, 3.5 m long, carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN and M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kN·m about the major axis. Use M20, Fe415, 8 mm ties, 40 mm cover and 20 mm bars on the two 300 mm faces. Find the steel and check it by strain compatibility.
steps: Minimum eccentricity: 3500/500 + 500/30 = 23.7 mm, so P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub> = 1200 × 0.0237 = 0.0 kN·m < 150 kN·m. Design for 150 kN·m.

Strain compatibility gives the steel that makes the curve pass through this point: A<sub>sc</sub> = 2097 mm², p = 1.40 %, p/f<sub>ck</sub> = 0.070. The SP 16 charts are drawn from the same theory, so a chart reading lands at about p/f<sub>ck</sub> ≈ 0.07.
Provide 8 bars of 20 mm, four on each 300 mm face: A<sub>sc</sub> = 2513 mm² (1.68 %).
Check at P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN: the neutral axis that gives this load is x<sub>u</sub> = 398.9 mm. Concrete: C = 0.36 × 20 × 300 × 398.9 = 861.6 kN at 0.416x<sub>u</sub> = 165.9 mm from the top.

Top bars (depth 58 mm): strain 0.0035 × (398.9 − 58)/398.9 = 0.00299, stress 353.8 − 8.9 (concrete displaced) = 344.9 N/mm², force 433.4 kN. Bottom bars (depth 442 mm): strain -0.00038, stress -75.6 N/mm² (tension), force -95.0 kN.
examples.answer: 8 bars of 20 mm (2513 mm², 1.68 %); at P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN the section resists 174 kN·m against 150 kN·m. Ties 8 mm at 300 mm c/c with links on the middle bars.

examples.question: A braced short corner column 400 mm × 400 mm, 3.0 m long, carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1500 kN, M<sub>ux</sub> = 120 kN·m and M<sub>uy</sub> = 90 kN·m. Use M25 and Fe415 with 8 equal bars (3 on each face). Check 8 bars of 20 mm, and redesign if needed.
steps: e<sub>min</sub> = 3000/500 + 400/30 = 19.3 mm → 20 mm, so the minimum moment is 1500 × 0.020 = 30 kN·m, below both applied moments.
Trial 8 bars of 20 mm: A<sub>sc</sub> = 2513 mm² (1.57 %). By symmetry M<sub>ux1</sub> = M<sub>uy1</sub>; at P<sub>u</sub> = 1500 kN strain compatibility gives 136.7 kN·m.

Try 8 bars of 25 mm: A<sub>sc</sub> = 3927 mm² (2.45 %), d′ = 60.5 mm. M<sub>ux1</sub> = M<sub>uy1</sub> = 183.5 kN·m at 1500 kN; P<sub>uz</sub> = 2978 kN; P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.504; αn = 1.506.
examples.answer: 8 bars of 20 mm fail the load contour (1.31); 8 bars of 25 mm (2.45 %) pass with 0.87. Ties: 8 mm at 300 mm c/c (16 × 25 = 400 mm and the 400 mm side do not govern).

traps: Reading M<sub>ux1</sub> at zero axial load. It must be the capacity at the design P<sub>u</sub>.
Taking αn as a constant 1.5 (or any guess). It comes from P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub>, between 1.0 and 2.0.
Writing P<sub>uz</sub> with A<sub>g</sub>. It is 0.45f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.75f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>, with the net concrete area.
Saying moment capacity always falls as axial load rises. Below the balanced load it rises.
Checking a circular column separately about x and y. Combine the moments as √(M<sub>ux</sub>² + M<sub>uy</sub>²) first.

quiz.q: Name the axes of an SP 16 column chart and its curve parameter.
quiz.a: Horizontal M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD²), vertical P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD); one curve for each p/f<sub>ck</sub>.

quiz.q: Give αn when P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub> is 0.15, 0.5 and 0.9.
Why does a small axial compression increase the moment capacity of a column section?
quiz.a: Below the balanced load the section fails by yielding of the tension steel. Axial compression lowers the tension in that steel, so a larger moment is needed before it yields. Above the balanced load the concrete crushes first, and more compression leaves less room for moment.

quiz.q: For a column, M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub> = 0.60, M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub> = 0.50 and P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.5. Check it.
For the 300 × 500 column of the first worked example, P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub> is needed in a biaxial check. Find P<sub>uz</sub>.
A 450 mm circular column carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN, M<sub>ux</sub> = 60 kN·m and M<sub>uy</sub> = 80 kN·m. What single moment is checked?
quiz.a: M<sub>u</sub> = √(60² + 80²) = 100 kN·m, about the resultant axis, at P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN.

quiz.q: In the second worked example the 25 mm bars raised P<sub>uz</sub> and so lowered αn. Did the lower αn help or hurt?
quiz.a: It hurt a little. For ratios below 1 a smaller exponent gives larger terms: with the 25 mm bars the ratios are 0.654 and 0.490; at the old αn = 1.646 the sum would be 0.807, at the new αn = 1.506 it is 0.869. The column passes because M<sub>u1</sub> rose from 137 to 183 kN·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design software draws the full three-dimensional interaction surface by fibre analysis of the section, so no load-contour exponent is needed, and it handles L-shaped and hollow sections too. Search for "fibre section analysis" and "P-M-M interaction surface".

figure.caption: Interaction curve of the uniaxial worked example’s 300 mm × 500 mm section with 8 bars of 20 mm (M20), by strain compatibility. The design point (150 kN·m, 1200 kN) lies inside; at that load the curve gives 174 kN·m.

A curve rises from pure bending at 178 kilonewton metres, bulges to 243 at the balanced load of 429 kilonewtons and returns to 2110 kilonewtons at zero moment. A dashed cap at 1879 kilonewtons, and the design point at 150 kilonewton metres and 1200 kilonewtons inside the curve, with the curve at 174.
